frequency spectra (SFS), which show how often newly derived variants occur at
different frequencies in a population, using TEVs and SNPs across the genome from
the four main groups”.
Line 202. The effect does not seem particularly strong, and it’s not clear that you
know that the higher number of rare TE variants is not due to low levels of TE
insertions. Further, since few readers will know what the directional coordinates
mean, it is not clear why there appears to be two classes of SNPs in the (0,1) group in
the histogram. It is also not clear if the authors mean SNPs within TEs (presumably
from unique single copy SNPs) or SNPs adjacent to the TEs. The problem
here is that the authors are making a clear statement concerning selection with a poorly described experiment.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comments. We agree that the observed
difference in site frequency spectra (SFS) between TEVs and SNPs is modest. We
performed this analysis using both SNPs and TEVs across the entire genome. To
improve clarity and avoid overstating conclusions, we have revised both the
manuscript and the figure. In the revision, we now write: “To estimate the effect of
TEVs on the genome, we analyzed the unfolded site frequency spectra (SFS), which
show how often newly derived variants occur at different frequencies in a population,
using TEVs and SNPs across the genome from the four main groups (Fig. 2g). In each
group, SNP frequencies showed a U-shaped distribution, whereas TEVs
demonstrated a lower proportion of fixed variants compared with SNPs”. We have
also removed the direct inference that the observed patterns are due to purifying
selection, to avoid overstating the conclusions based on the current evidence.
Line 204. This is a strong claim that should be supported by the evidence.
Response: Thank you for your comment. We agree that our current evidence, based
on genotype–environment association (GEA) analyses, supports associations between
TEVs and traits related to local adaptation, but does not provide direct experimental
validation of their causal roles. To avoid overstating our conclusions, we have revised
the section title: Potential role of TEVs in local adaptation of Amur grape.
Line 216. Given that I am not familiar with these models, I am going to assume that
these include Bonferoni corrections.
Response: Yes, these models include Bonferroni corrections, which are illustrated in
figure 3 and supplementary figure S10.
Line 226. Given the dramatic differences in recombination frequency in different
parts of plant genomes, I am surprised that a map unit distance wasn’t used instead of
a generic number of base pairs.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We acknowledge that
recombination rates can vary significantly across different regions of plant genomes.
In our study, the 20 kb window upstream and downstream of adaptive candidate
variants was selected based on the linkage disequilibrium (LD) decay pattern
observed in Amur grape. Considering the observed LD decay, this physical distance
was deemed an appropriate proxy to capture genomic regions potentially linked to the
candidate variants. We chose this approach because a high-resolution genetic map for
Amur grape is currently unavailable.
Line 226. “adaptive candidate variants” should be candidate adaptive variants.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We have revised this term in our
manuscript.
Line 230. “The gene TLP3 was” You mean the grape homolog of this gene” (same
below)
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We have revised the manuscript
accordingly. Specifically, we now refer to “The Amur grape homolog of TLP3 …” to
clarify this point.
Line 234. “in the putative cis-region of the gene TLP3”. It is demonstrably cis. I think
you mean putative cis regulatory region.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. We agree that “putative cis-
regulatory region” is a more precise term, and we have revised the manuscript
accordingly.
Line 247. “The gene HHP4” should be “allelic variation in”
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. We have revised the manuscript
to specify “allelic variation in the gene HHP4” to more accurately reflect the
association.
Line 248. “described in response to” should be “has been implicated in...” Also, does
the reference actually show this?
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We agree that “has been implicated
in” is a more accurate expression than “has been described in response to.” We have
revised the sentence accordingly. Regarding the reference, we have carefully
rechecked it and confirmed that it supports the involvement of the HHP gene family
in response to temperature and salt stress.
Line 251. “associated with variant in temperature seasonality” should be variation in.
Here and throughout, please check grammar.
Response: Thank you for your helpful comment. We have corrected “associated with
variant in temperature seasonality” to “associated with variation in temperature
seasonality” and have carefully checked the manuscript for similar grammatical issues
throughout.
Line 252. “putative cis-region” Again, you mean putative cis regulatory region.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We have revised this term in our
manuscript.
Line 253. Again, grammar actually matters for meaning. “ illustrate the relationship
between the allele frequency.” You did not mean that in order to illustrate something,
you identified this particular SNP, I assume, but that is what the text as written says. I
suspect you mean that you are talking about this SNP because it is the best candidate.
Response: Thank you for pointing out the ambiguity in our original sentence. To
clarify, we have revised the sentence: “We selected the candidate adaptive SNP
(SNP14_26191757, representing a G-to-A substitution), located in the putative cis-
regulatory region (ca. 1kb upstream of the 5’UTR) of the gene ICE1, as the best
example to illustrate the relationship between the allele frequency and the
environmental variable”.
Line 263. “We estimated the proportion of environmental variance (PVE) explained
by...” Again, as written, this is incorrect. You are not explaining the proportion of
environmental variance by genetic variation because the environmental variance
occurs independently of the genetic variance.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We agree that environmental
variance and genetic variance are independent. We have revised the sentence as:
“We estimated the proportion of environmental variance (PVE) associated with different
genetic variants”.
Line 267. What is meant by “exclusive” here? That this is variance that would be
wholly missed if only SNPs were used?
Response: Thank you for your comment. By “exclusive contribution”, we refer to the
proportion of the environmental variance uniquely attributable to TEVs, which would
not be captured if only SNPs and indels were considered. We have revised the text to
clarify this as follows: “Notably, the unique contribution of TEVs to most
environmental variables was larger than that of both SNPs and indels in this study”.
Line 279. To be clear, does this mean that you picked variants that co-occurred under
similar conditions, or that co-occurred in localized geographic regions? The first
would be more interesting I would think because it would get around population
structure differences.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We mean variants that were
consistently identified as associated with the same six uncorrelated environmental
variables (bio4, elev, bio15, bio3, bio18, and bio10) by both LFMM and redundancy
analysis (RDA). These variants were considered “core adaptive variants” for local
adaptation. We have clarified this in the revised manuscript.
Line 283. Here and throughout, just a bit of explanation would be helpful for many
readers. Here I assume you are saying that you looked at all the various local
populations, the amount of variation that you surmise will be important for adaptation
in response to two possible climate change (based on the relationship to that variation
and current conditions), and then assessed the vulnerability of those populations. ]
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. We assessed the genomic
vulnerability of Amur grape populations by analyzing adaptive genetic variants linked
to current environments. We then projected how these populations might respond to
future climate scenarios (SSP245 and SSP585) in two periods by estimating the
genetic offset, which reflects the mismatch between current adaptation and future
conditions. We have added a brief explanation in the revised manuscript for clarity:
“This involved estimating the genetic offset, which measures the mismatch between
current adaptive genetic variation and the genetic composition needed under future
climate conditions, to assess potential population maladaptation.”
Line 287. “Populations with higher genetic offsets” I assume that means populations
with lower frequencies of alleles that would facilitate adaptation?
Response: Thank you for your comment. To clarify, populations with higher genetic
offsets have a larger mismatch between their current genetic composition and that
required for future climate adaptation. This does not necessarily mean they currently
have lower frequencies of adaptive alleles, but rather that greater changes in allele
frequencies will be necessary to achieve adaptation. We hope this clarifies the
concept.
Line 290. This kind of goes without saying doesn’t it? What would be more
informative would be if the differences between vulnerable and more adaptive
populations would be exacerbated.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. We agree that the increase in
genetic vulnerability over time is expected and may be somewhat redundant to state.
Therefore, we have removed this sentence from the revised manuscript to improve
clarity.
Line 304. I think you mean “may play and important role”. I am surprised that the
adapative SNPs essentially made no difference. Does this make sense based on the
distribution of the effects of the SNPs? That is, since we know that many of the
SNPs are linked to potentially adaptive traits, is it those case that these are unlikely to be those that would facilitate
adaptation to the particular conditions predicted by these models?
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We agree that “may play an
important role” is a more cautious expression, and we have revised the manuscript
accordingly. In our study, we focused on evaluating the potential role of TEVs in
future climate adaptation. The baseline set of adaptive SNPs and indels served as a
reference for comparison, but this does not imply that SNPs and indels have little
importance in predicting future adaptation. Our results highlight that TEVs provide
additional, complementary adaptive variation that further reduces genetic offset
beyond what is captured by SNPs and indels alone. We have revised the manuscript
as follows: “To explore the role of TEVs in shaping the adaptive potential of Amur
grape under future climate change, we estimated genetic offsets using LD-pruned
adaptive TEVs, SNPs, and indels. We specifically assessed the potential role of TEVs
by comparing models that included LD-pruned adaptive TEVs alongside SNPs and
indels (adaptive TEVs set) with those using only LD-pruned adaptive SNPs and indels
(baseline set). Across all periods and emission scenarios, the baseline set showed
significantly higher genetic offsets (all Ps < 0.003), whereas inclusion of TEVs
reduced offsets by 7.3–8.2% (Supplementary Table S13). Results from different
datasets showed similar spatial and temporal genetic offset patterns (Fig. 4 and
Supplementary Figs. S13-S15). Populations of the Northeast group showed relatively
high genetic offsets, indicating greater vulnerability to future climate change
(supplementary Fig. S15). As a control, the average genetic offsets based on random
non-adaptive TEVs plus LD-pruned adaptive SNPs and indels (control set) showed no
significant difference from the baseline set (Fig. 4c). These findings suggested that
adaptive TEVs may play an important role in future climate adaptation of Amur grape
by providing complementary adaptive genetic variation that reduces genetic offset”.
Line 326. They do not reveal that TEVs significantly enhance the plants' adaptive
potential to climate change, they show that your model suggests this. The map, as
they say, is not the terrain. Given that climate change as already significantly affected
growing conditions, I wonder if you could make some retrospective predictions.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. You are correct that our results are based
on model predictions rather than direct empirical evidence, and our wording may have
overstated this point. We have revised the sentence to clarify that our findings indicate
that TEVs may enhance the adaptive potential of Amur grape under future climate
scenarios, as suggested by our modeling results: “Secondly, using a machine learning
model, we predicted the spatiotemporal adaptability of Amur grape populations to
future climate change, with the results suggesting that TEVs may enhance their
adaptive potential to climate change”.
Regarding retrospective predictions, we agree this would be an interesting approach to
further validate the model, but such an analysis would require detailed historical
genomic datasets as control, which are currently unavailable for Amur grape. We
acknowledge this as a potential avenue for future research.
Line 339. “ hotspots of genetic variant in” should be “variation”, not variant.
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We agree with your suggestion and have
changed “hotspots of genetic variant” to “hotspots of genetic variation” in the revised
manuscript.
Line 345. However is the beginning of a new sentence here. Also, please check
throughout for the distinction between variant and variation.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We have corrected the sentence.
Additionally, we carefully checked the manuscript and ensured consistent and
appropriate use of “variant” and “variation” throughout the text.
Line 353. Is there evidence for recent mobilization of TEs in these populations? One
thing of particular interest would be the way that the TEs were profiled. Most
importantly, if there were multiple copies of identical TEs, were they all counted?
I assume so, because you are looking for polymorphic insertions, but I am concerned
about whether or not they were missed. Given the centrality of TEs in this analysis, I
am also surprised that the authors did not look carefully at the population structure of
the TEs themselves.
Response: Thank you for raising these important points. To address the possibility of
recent mobilization, we estimated TE insertion times based on RepeatMasker outputs.
Our results indicated a broad peak of TE activity around ~5 Mya, followed by a sharp
decline in more recent insertions, suggesting that most TE insertions are relatively
ancient rather than recently active (Supplementary Fig. S2b). Regarding duplicate
copies, each TEV was indeed counted individually so that no polymorphic insertions
were missed. Finally, we performed a population structure analysis based on TEVs,
and the results were highly concordant with those obtained from SNPs (Fig. S4),
confirming that the TE dataset reliably reflects the underlying population history.
Line 363. I would caution the authors to use correct terminology when discussion
evolution. Species don’t adapt to anything “in order to” do anything. Evolution is
simply what happens. Species don’t have agency.
Response: Thank you for your valuable comment. We agree that the original wording
is inappropriate. To address this, we have removed the sentence “To avoid extinction,
species employ adaptive strategies in response to climate change, e.g. undergoing
genetic evolution or moving to new suitable habitats” from the manuscript.
Line 397. These are all great examples, but given the large number of candidates that
are just above the significance plot in 3d, as is ICE, how is the reader to know that
there are so many genes involved in various stress responses, the authors would
inevitably find at least some of them? I do understand that much of this is “under the
hood” of the various algorithms, but it might be helpful for the authors to carefully
spell out why these candidates are unlikely to have been identified by chance?
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment. To address the concern about the
possibility of false positives among candidate genes, we would like to clarify two
points. First, we applied a stringent statistical significance threshold (False Discovery
Rate, FDR < 0.01), which is more rigorous than the commonly used FDR < 0.05 in
many other studies, thereby minimizing the chance of false positives in our analyses.
Second, many of the identified genes have well-documented functional roles in stress
responses, supported by previous experimental evidence. Specifically, some adaptive
genes we identified, such as BAM3, ICE1, and CBF, have been functionally validated
in Amur grape, providing strong cross-study support for our findings.
Line 419. These are excellent points.
Response: Thank you for your kind words. We appreciate your recognition of our
findings on the role of TEVs in adaptation.
Line 486. In the text of the M&M, this is everything about how TEs were identified:
Transposable element families were identified by RepeatModeler with a pan-Vitis
database of repeat families. The repeat elements were
classified by using deepTE with the Plant model. Finally, we annotated all repetitive
sequences using RepeatMasker (v4.1.2). TEs are notoriously difficult to accurately
identify and TEs are at the core of this analysis. I will return to this comment later, but
the process if far more involved that simply using a few out of the box tool sets.
Response: Thank you for your insightful comment regarding the identification of
TEs. We acknowledge that TE annotation is a challenging and complex process. In
our study, we employed a comprehensive and widely used pipeline combining
RepeatModeler, deepTE classification, and RepeatMasker annotation, which together
provide high accuracy and reliability. We believe that the quality and depth of our TE
identification are sufficient to support the analyses and conclusions presented in this
manuscript.
Figure 2, line 1009. The wording here is unclear. “based on genes with a frequency
more than 80% of TEVs in the CDS region” Does that mean genes that, on average,
among all the accessions, 80% of them have a TE insertion into the CDS?
Presumably, these are pseudogenes, TEs that look like genes, or just bad calls by
annotation programs, which are often inaccurate. I would assume that these “genes”
also have much higher rates of non-synonymous point mutations as well. Do they?
Response: Thank you for pointing this out. We realize that our original wording in the
figure legend was ambiguous. To clarify, what we mean is: we performed gene
ontology (GO) analysis on genes containing TEVs with an allele frequency > 0.8 in
their CDS regions. It does not mean that 80% of the CDS is occupied by TE
sequences, nor that 80% of the genes have such insertions. We have revised the figure
legend to read: “Gene ontology (GO) analysis of genes containing TEVs (allele
frequency > 0.8) in their CDS regions”.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors present a pan-genome analysis of Vitis amurensis, offering novel insight
into the role of transposable elements in environmental adaptation. While the study
has clear potential, several key issues need to be addressed before it can be considered
for publication:
1. The population structure analysis indicates that the South clade possesses a distinct
genetic background, as further supported by syntenic and PCA analyses. These results
suggest that the South clade may represent a separate evolutionary lineage, potentially
not belonging to V. amurensis. The authors should provide additional taxonomic
evidence (e.g., morphological traits) or molecular validation to clarify the
classification of these accessions.
Response: Thank you for this important comment. We have examined the
morphological traits of accessions from all four V. amurensis clades, including the
South clade, and have added representative images in Supplementary Figure S3. No
obvious morphological differences were observed among the four clades based on the
taxonomic characteristics of V. amurensis as described in the Flora of China.
Therefore, based on morphological evidence, the South clade is morphologically
consistent with V. amurensis.
2. Although the study identifies genes potentially associated with environmental
adaptation, the analysis is based solely on LFMM modeling using climatic variables.
To comprehensively identify genes involved in cold/drought stress responses,
phenotypic data across all accessions should be incorporated. A phenotype-genotype
association analysis would offer more direct and biologically relevant evidence for
adaptive traits.
Response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We fully agree that incorporating
phenotype–genotype association analyses using cold- and drought-tolerance
phenotypic data across all accessions would provide more direct and biologically
relevant evidence for adaptive traits. However, such comprehensive phenotypic
datasets are currently unavailable for the full set of accessions included in this study
and obtaining them would require extensive multi-year common garden and
controlled-environment experiments. In this work, we therefore focused on
genotype–environment associations as a well-established approach to identify
putative adaptive loci in the absence of large-scale phenotypic measurements. We
agree that integrating phenotype–genotype analyses in future research will be an
important next step to further validate the adaptive roles of the identified genes.
3. While the LFMM analysis identified numbers of significant genetic variants, the
author only focused on a subset of genes related to cold and drought resistance. Genes
linked to other significant loci should also be listed and considered. Additionally, the
wild habitats of the accessions should be clearly documented, along with the
corresponding environmental factors of those habitats, to ensure the accuracy and
relevance of the analysis. It is also important to verify that the sampled accessions
originate from natural populations rather than cultivated sources; such as individuals
maintained in germplasm resource gardens should be traceable to their native habitat.
Response: We appreciate your valuable suggestions. Following your
recommendation, we have now listed all genes linked to significant loci, not only
those related to cold and drought resistance, in Supplementary Tables S7–S12. We
also confirm that all accessions analyzed in this study were collected from wild
populations in their natural habitats. Detailed information on the wild habitats of these
accessions, along with the corresponding environmental factors, is now provided in
Supplementary Table S6.
4. The author state that “Transposable elements mediate adaptation to environment
change” and identify several genes associated with cold and drought resistance.
However, the manuscript lacks a detailed genetic or regulatory model explaining how
these genes contribute to environmental adaption. The authors should provide
mechanistic insights or supporting evidence to support this conclusion.
Response: We appreciate your valuable suggestions. In the revised manuscript, we
further explored the potential functional relevance of environment-associated variants.
We examined the genomic context of candidate loci using the PlantCARE database to
predict cis-regulatory elements, including promoter motifs and transcription factor
binding sites. This allowed us to evaluate whether sequence variants might alter
regulatory motifs and thereby influence gene expression. For instance, we found a TE
insertion upstream of TLP3 that overlaps a predicted transcription factor binding site,
as well as a SNP upstream of ICE1 located within a putative regulatory motif. These
findings suggest that environment-associated variants could contribute to adaptation
by modulating regulatory networks (see revised Results and Supplementary Fig. S9).
Our findings provide a valuable set of testable hypotheses and candidate loci for
future functional studies.
In addition, we tone down the title to avoid overinterpretation, we have revised the
title to: Transposable Elements Contribute to Climate Change Adaptation in Wild
Grapes,” which more accurately reflects the content of our analyses.
** See Nature Portfolio’s author and referees' website at www.nature.com/authors for
information about policies, services and author benefits.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I appreciate the detailed answer to my comments from the authors.
I only have a few minor comments remaining:
L151-156: I am still not sure whether the pangenome graph is well introduced or well placed. The first section of the results
describes the genome assemblies and suddenly switches to “To better detect structural variants” while no population
genetic results were presented yet. Also, the title of the section is “Graph-based pangenome reference for Amur grape
(Vampan_V1.0)” while it is only briefly presented in the last two sentences. Same for the Figure 1, it is entitled “Graph-based
pangenome reference (Vampan_V1.0) for Amur grape” while none of the results presented are related to the pangenome
graph. Please rename the first results section and the Figure 1 so they do not refer to the pangenome. For better logical flow,
please move the 2 sentences about the pangenome L151-156 into the next section when you use the structural variant
analysis to complement your linear genome SNP analysis right before “The utilization of a pangenome for Amur grape”
L174.
L531: How the bam files were filtered?
L533: Please give more details about the variant call, which GATK function did you use? How did you merge the results
from all the samples? How did you extract SNP and indel from the variant call?
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
Thanks to the authors for their thoughtful responses to my previous comments.
I think my ongoing concerns have much more to do with framing and assertions of what has been shown to be the case than
the quality of the data. I don’t know if this is a language think or a scientific culture thing, but by my lights you can’t say
you’ve demonstrated a conclusion just because you provide evidence supporting that conclusion. For instance, the authors
state that: “We evaluate the role of TEVs in facilitating local adaptation of Amur grape to current and future climates, with
implications for its survival in a rapidly changing environment.” But they did not really evaluate the role of TEVs in future
climates, they provided evidence that they may play a role in facilitating adaptation to future changes. They did not detect
246 adaptive variants; they detected 246 putative adaptive variants.
“Our results demonstrate that adaptive TEVs significantly reduce genetic offsets of populations with 7.3% to 8.2% reduction
amplitude, indicating these variants play an important role in enhancing local adaptation to future climate change.” The
language here is difficult to follow. The putative, adaptive TEVs reduce genetic offsets of populations that that ave 7.3% to
8.2% amplitude, or they reduce the genetic offsets by 7.3 to 8.2%. An X% reduction amplitude is not a meaningful phrase.
Line 124. Might be a good place to carefully define “genetic offset” here, since it’s important for your overall argument.
Line 201. As I understand it, “fixed” means 100%.
Line 206. These are also classes of genes that are often present in relatively large numbers, many members of which may
not be functional, subject to relaxed selection and colocalized with TE insertions because the insertions don’t have an effect
on phenotype. Also, in figure 2g, the results are somewhat underwhelming. The actual total number of genes is very small,
and the largest class has a very low p value. Honestly, if I am reading the figure correctly, these dots (whose color I cannot
see) represent less than seven genes; how could you end up with anything like a significant result from so few genes? Am I
missing something? And why are you focusing on insertions in the CDS regions? Because knockouts would be more likely
to contribute to adaptation?
Figure 1c. What are the colors here? What do they correspond to? I get that they correspond to the various haplotypes but
please make it obvious for the non-specialist.
Line 212. Reference for use of this? I’m sure it’s a common measure, but it would be nice to see an example of how this was
used in a similar situation.
Line 235. As below, please refer to these as “potentially adaptive” variants.
Line 279. Here and throughout, consider avoiding this kind of passive wording. “Were considered” can mean that someone
else in the past thought this, or that the authors did, or that they do. Here I assume that the authors are hypothesizing that
these are good candidates based on linkage and their presumed function.
Line 286. Both together or individually?
Line 288. Again, the language is a real problem here and must be addressed. The TEVs didn’t “account” for variance in the
precipitation of “warmest quarter”; I’m not even certain what this means. Genetic variation associated with the population in
the warmest quarter?
Line 292. Again, the wording suggests that you know that these variants are responsible for “adaptation”. You don’t know
that. All you have is linkage and a hypothesis.
Line 306. This is pure supposition. The authors, indeed, no one knows what variation will prove to be adaptive. I would
accept a far more watered down version of this that spelled out very carefully the logic, which, I assume, is that if we accept
that the variation present now is associated with and required for current adaptation, this might tell us about what kinds of
variation are currently available for future adaptation.
Line 349. I’m afraid I am unconvince that the authors have shown “the critical role of TEVs in adaptive evolution and suggest
that comprehensive population genomics research is essential for developing effective breeding and conservation strategies
for crops and their wild relatives in the face of climate change.” They have provided some interesting evidence for this, but
that’s it.
Line 359. They may have also been purged from regions with higher levels of conservation.
Line 418. These are all interesting possibilities, but so far, I am concerned that these are simply “just so” stories.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors have partially addressed my concerns. However, they have evaded several key issues, which continues to
undermine the ability to effectively guarantee the article’s accuracy and scientific rigor. Given this incomplete resolution, I
still have the following unresolved concerns and questions that require further clarification:
1. we have located the images in Supplementary Figure S3. While the figures are accessible, the authors should provide
standardized, professional images for different groups, as the currently provided materials appear to have been captured in a
relatively casual and unstandardized manner. Such non-professional imagery may introduce ambiguity and ultimately affect
the reliability of the visual evidence presented.
2. Upon examining the phenotypes of these germplasms, we identified a substantial number of identical environmental
phenotypes. This observation strongly suggests that either the phenotypic data separation is unreliable or the samples were
collected within an overly restricted geographical range. Compounding this issue, the bio5 (Max Temperature of the
Warmest Month) values range from 23℃ to 31℃, which is inconsistent with prevailing climatic conditions. Therefore, the
authors must first provide a detailed explanation for this discrepancy and then offer empirical evidence to verify the data’s
accuracy. Furthermore, despite the authors’ previous explanation regarding environmental factors, these factors alone
cannot adequately reflect the true adaptability of these germplasm resources. To ensure the validity of the analysis,
intrinsic grape phenotypes that are directly indicative of environmental adaptability should therefore be supplemented.
3. While the authors have presented some preliminary analyses of transposons, the relationship between transposons and
resistance or environmental adaptation remains inadequately defined. As this constitutes the core proposition of the
manuscript, further in-depth analysis and supplementary data are imperative to strengthen the argument. Moreover, the
manuscript lacks a detailed genetic or regulatory model that elucidates how the identified genes mediate environmental
adaptation. Building on this gap, the authors are therefore urged to provide mechanistic insights or additional corroborative
evidence to substantiate this key conclusion and enhance the overall persuasiveness of the study.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
Response to Review Comments
Part I: Summary of responses to the major questions:
We sincerely appreciate the interest shown by the editor and the three reviewers. Before
presenting a detailed point-by-point response in Part II, we first address three major
issues collectively:
First, enhanced result organization and methodological clarity: We reorganized
the Results section to introduce the pangenome graph in a more logical order, aligning
its presentation with subsequent analyses. The Methods section was expanded with
detailed descriptions of BAM file filtering and GATK-based variant-calling
procedures to enhance analytical reproducibility.
Second, clarified TEVs’ potential role using cautious language: We revised the
manuscript to use cautious phrasing, replacing assertive terms (e.g., “adaptive
variants”) with cautious phrasing (“putative adaptive variants”) and clarifying TEVs’
potential role in adaptation to future climates.
Third, improvements in figure quality and data validation: We updated
Supplementary Figure S3 with standardized, high-resolution leaf images and scale
bars to improve visual clarity and comparability across population groups. We also
clarified our sampling design, environmental data resolution, and the rationale for
population-level analyses to address concerns regarding data reliability and accuracy.
In conclusion, we have provided detailed explanations in response to the reviewers'
comments. All updates in the manuscript are highlighted with tracked changes.
Additionally, we have revised the manuscript and supplemental figures.
Part II: Point by point response to specific comments:
(The reviewer’s comments are shown in black, and the authors’ responses are
displayed in blue.)
REVIEWER COMMENTS
Reviewer #1 (Remarks to the Author):
I appreciate the detailed answer to my comments from the authors.
I only have a few minor comments remaining:
L151-156: I am still not sure whether the pangenome graph is well introduced or well
placed. The first section of the results describes the genome assemblies and suddenly
switches to “To better detect structural variants” while no population genetic results
were presented yet. Also, the title of the section is “Graph-based pangenome reference
for Amur grape (Vampan_V1.0)” while it is only briefly presented in the last two
sentences. Same for the Figure 1, it is entitled “Graph-based pangenome reference
(Vampan_V1.0) for Amur grape” while none of the results presented are related to the
pangenome graph. Please rename the first results section and the Figure 1 so they do
not refer to the pangenome. For better logical flow, please move the 2 sentences about
the pangenome L151-156 into the next section when you use the structural variant
analysis to complement your linear genome SNP analysis right before “The utilization
of a pangenome for Amur grape” L174.
Response: Thank you for pointing out this issue of logical flow and section labeling.
Following your suggestion, we renamed the first Results section to “Haplotype-
resolved genome assemblies and TE landscape of Amur grape” and retitled Figure 1
as “Morphology, genome assemblies, and population structure of Amur grape”.

only high-quality primary alignments before downstream processing. Specifically, we
used the following command: samtools view -bS -F 0x100 -q 10, which removes
secondary alignments and retains reads with a mapping quality greater than 10. The
resulting BAM files were then sorted using samtools, and PCR duplicates were
identified and marked with Picard MarkDuplicates.
The revised sentence now reads: “BAM files were filtered using samtools view -bS -F
0x100 -q 10 to remove secondary alignments and low-quality reads. The filtered
BAM files were then sorted with SAMtools (v1.13), and PCR duplicates were
identified and marked using Picard (v2.23.0) MarkDuplicates
(http://broadinstitute.github.io/picard/).”
L533: Please give more details about the variant call, which GATK function did you
use? How did you merge the results from all the samples? How did you extract SNP
and indel from the variant call?

“The SNP and indel calling was performed using GATK (v4.2.6.0) functions of
HaplotypeCaller, GenomicsDBImport, GenotypeGVCFs, SelectVariants and
VariantFiltration. Specifically, variants were called per sample using HaplotypeCaller
in GVCF mode to generate individual GVCF files. All GVCF files were combined
with GenomicsDBImport to build a genomic database, and joint genotyping across all
samples was performed using GenotypeGVCFs to produce cohort-level VCF files for
each chromosome. The SNPs and indels were extracted from the joint VCF files using
SelectVariants with the options -select-type SNP and -select-type INDEL,
respectively. These variant sets were then filtered using VariantFiltration. SNPs were
filtered based on “QD<2.0 || FS >60.0 || MQRankSum <- 12.5 || ReadPosRankSum <-
8.0 || SOR >3.0 || MQ<40.0”, while Indels were filtered using “QD<2.0 || FS >200.0 ||
MQRankSum <- 12.5 || ReadPosRankSum <- 8.0 || SOR >10.0”. The resulting
variants were filtered by VCFtools (v0.1.15) using parameters: -max-missing 0.8”.
Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
Thanks to the authors for their thoughtful responses to my previous comments.
I think my ongoing concerns have much more to do with framing and assertions of
what has been shown to be the case than the quality of the data. I don’t know if this is
a language think or a scientific culture thing, but by my lights you can’t say
you’ve demonstrated a conclusion just because you provide evidence supporting that
conclusion. For instance, the authors state that: “We evaluate the role of TEVs in
facilitating local adaptation of Amur grape to current and future climates, with
implications for its survival in a rapidly changing environment.” But they did not
really evaluate the role of TEVs in future climates, they provided evidence that they

revised manuscript, we have carefully refined the language throughout to more
accurately reflect the strength and scope of our evidence. For example, we now state
that we “evaluated the potential role of TEVs in facilitating local adaptation of V.
amurensis to current and projected future climates” and that “TEVs may play a role in
facilitating adaptation of populations to future climate change”. In addition, we now
refer to the identified loci as “putative adaptive variants” rather than “adaptive
variants.” Similar revisions have been made across the Abstract, Introduction, Results,
and Discussion to ensure cautious and appropriate framing.

populations with 7.3% to 8.2% reduction amplitude, indicating these variants play an
important role in enhancing local adaptation to future climate change.” The language
here is difficult to follow. The putative, adaptive TEVs reduce genetic offsets of

Response: Thank you for pointing out this ambiguity. We have revised the sentence to
clarify its meaning and improve readability. The revised version now reads: “Our
results indicate that putative adaptive TEVs significantly reduce population genetic
offsets by 7.3% to 8.2%, suggesting that these variants may contribute to enhancing
local adaptation to future climate change.”
Line 124. Might be a good place to carefully define “genetic offset” here, since it’s
important for your overall argument.
Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We agree that defining “genetic
offset” will improve clarity for readers unfamiliar with this concept. We have
therefore revised the text to include a brief definition. The revised sentence now
reads: “quantify and estimate the vulnerability of populations by assessing genetic
offset (i.e., the predicted genomic mismatch between current and future climate
scenarios)”.
Line 201. As I understand it, “fixed” means 100%.
Response: Thank you for this clarification. Our intention was to indicate that these
TEVs show very high frequencies within populations. We have revised the sentence
to: “TEVs with a population frequency great than 0.8 in the CDS regions are likely
under positive selection in natural populations”.
Line 206. These are also classes of genes that are often present in relatively large
numbers, many members of which may not be functional, subject to relaxed selection
and colocalized with TE insertions because the insertions don’t have an effect on

We focused on TEVs located in CDS regions because these regions are highly
conserved, and TEVs (including insertions or deletions) within them can alter amino

implications for environmental adaptation. While TEVs in non-coding regions may
also be functionally relevant, our focus on CDS regions reflects their higher
likelihood of producing measurable functional effects.
We agree that these genes classes may be subject to relaxed selection or may
colocalize with TE insertions without having direct phenotypic effects. To address

any implication of causality.
The revised sentence now reads: “TEVs with a population frequency greater than 0.8
in the CDS regions are likely under positive selection in natural populations (Fig. 2e).
To explore their potential functional impact, we performed gene ontology (GO)

to defense response (P = 0.0078), defense response to other organism (P = 1.99e-4),

with whole-genome LD-pruned SNPs. Four major geographic groups were identified:
Northeast (red), Center (orange), West (blue) and South (green).”
Line 212. Reference for use of this? I’m sure it’s a common measure, but it would be

Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have added relevant references
to illustrate the application of the unfolded site frequency spectrum (SFS) in similar

PNAS 2023). These references provide examples of similar comparable analytical

accordingly and now refer to these as “putative adaptive variants” to more accurately

Line 279. Here and throughout, consider avoiding this kind of passive wording. “Were

Response: Thank you for this valuable suggestion. We agree that “were considered”

we have replaced it with more precise expressions such as “were defined as,” or

Response: Thank you for pointing out this ambiguity. We have clarified the sentence
to specify the comparison. The revised version now reads: “Notably, the unique
contribution of TEVs to most environmental variables was larger than that of SNPs or
indels when compared individually.”
Line 288. Again, the language is a real problem here and must be addressed. The
TEVs didn’t “account” for variance in the precipitation of “warmest quarter”; I’m not

Response: Thank you for this valuable comment and for catching the imprecise
phrasing. What we intended to express is that TEVs explained a portion of the genetic
variation associated with the environmental variable (bio18, precipitation of the
warmest quarter). We have revised the sentence accordingly for clarity.
The revised version now reads: “TEVs uniquely explained 11.12% of the genetic
variation associated with precipitation of the warmest quarter, a much larger
proportion than that explained by SNPs or indels.”

Response: Thank you for this important clarification. To avoid overstating our
conclusions, we have revised the text to use more cautious wording.
The revised sentences now read: “TEVs were still identified as associated with these
environmental variables (Supplementary Fig. S11). These results suggest that TEVs
may contribute to ecological adaptation in Amur grape, representing a previously
overlooked component of adaptive genetic diversity.”
Line 306. This is pure supposition. The authors, indeed, no one knows what variation

difficulty in determining which variants will truly be adaptive in the future. In our

informative assessment of potential adaptive capacity. In the revised version, we have

now describe these genes as “candidate genes potentially associated with
environmental adaptation” based on their known homologs and prior studies.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors have partially addressed my concerns. However, they have evaded
several key issues, which continues to undermine the ability to effectively guarantee
the article’s accuracy and scientific rigor. Given this incomplete resolution, I still have
the following unresolved concerns and questions that require further clarification:
1. we have located the images in Supplementary Figure S3. While the figures are
accessible, the authors should provide standardized, professional images for different
groups, as the currently provided materials appear to have been captured in a
relatively casual and unstandardized manner. Such non-professional imagery may
introduce ambiguity and ultimately affect the reliability of the visual evidence
presented.
Response: Thank you for this helpful suggestion. We have replaced the previous
images in Supplementary Figure S3 with standardized photographs of representative
leaves from different population groups. Each image was captured under consistent
background conditions, with a scale bar added to indicate size. These revisions ensure
a more professional and comparable presentation of morphological characteristics
across groups, thereby improving the clarity and reliability of the visual evidence.
Thank you once again for your constructive feedback.
2. Upon examining the phenotypes of these germplasms, we identified a substantial
number of identical environmental phenotypes. This observation strongly suggests
that either the phenotypic data separation is unreliable or the samples were
collected within an overly restricted geographical range. Compounding this issue, the
bio5 (Max Temperature of the Warmest Month) values range from 23℃ to 31℃, which is
inconsistent with prevailing climatic conditions. Therefore, the authors must first
provide a detailed explanation for this discrepancy and then offer empirical evidence
to verify the data’s accuracy. Furthermore, despite the authors’ previous explanation
regarding environmental factors, these factors alone cannot adequately reflect the true
adaptability of these germplasm resources. To ensure the validity of the analysis,
intrinsic grape phenotypes that are directly indicative of environmental adaptability
should therefore be supplemented.
Response: Thank you for this important comment. We would like to clarify several
points regarding our sampling strategy, environmental data, and analytical rationale.
Our sampling strategy was designed to comprehensively cover the full geographical
and climatic range of the Amur grape, encompassing 330 individuals from 31 natural
populations spanning over 20 degrees in latitude (Fig. 1f). Within each population,
individuals were sampled at a minimum distance of 100 meters to minimize the
collection of clones or closely related individuals.
All environmental variables were obtained from WorldClim (www.worldclim.org) at a
resolution of 2.5 arcmin (~5 km). Because this dataset assigns identical environmental
values to sampling locations within a single grid cell, individuals from the same
population often share identical environmental data. This is a known characteristic of
the dataset and has been widely adopted in population genomic studies using
genotype–environment association analyses (e.g., Sang et al., Nat. Commun., 2022;
Zhang et al., Mol. Plant, 2024). Since our analyses are conducted at the population
level, rather than at the level of individual microenvironments, this does not
compromise the validity of our results.
Regarding the reviewer’s concern about the bio5 (Max Temperature of the Warmest
Month), we have carefully verified these values and confirmed their accuracy in
WorldClim. The observed range reflects our inclusion of high-latitude and high-
altitude forest populations (Fig 1f and supplementary tables S6), where maximum
summer temperatures are naturally moderated relative to surrounding lowland areas.
We agree with the reviewer that experimental validation using intrinsic plant
phenotypes would provide the most direct evidence of environmental adaptation. In
this study, we employed a genotype–environment association approach based on the
rationale that the survival of wild populations in specific ecological niches reflects
underlying local adaptation. By correlating genomic variation with environmental
variables, we identified candidate loci potentially involved in adaptation. The
effectiveness of this strategy is supported by our identification of several genes with
known roles in abiotic stress tolerance (e.g., ICE1 and BAM3, which were confirmed
as confirmed
as key regulators of freezing tolerance in Amur grape), indicating that our approach
captures biologically relevant signals. While phenotypic data would strengthen our
conclusions, generating such data for 330 accessions would require extensive multi-
year experiments beyond the current scope. This study provides a comprehensive
adaptive landscape for the Amur grape, offering a foundation for future functional
validation and breeding efforts. We believe your constructive suggestion represents a
valuable direction for subsequent research.
Reference:
Sang, Y. P. et al. Genomic insights into local adaptation and future climate-induced
vulnerability of a keystone forest tree in East Asia. Nat Commun. 13, 6541 (2022).
Zhang, F. et al. Evolutionary genomics of climatic adaptation and resilience to climate
change in alfalfa. Mol Plant 17, 867-883 (2024).
3. While the authors have presented some preliminary analyses of transposons, the
relationship between transposons and resistance or environmental adaptation remains
inadequately defined. As this constitutes the core proposition of the manuscript,
further in-depth analysis and supplementary data are imperative to strengthen the
argument. Moreover, the manuscript lacks a detailed genetic or regulatory model that
elucidates how the identified genes mediate environmental adaptation. Building on
this gap, the authors are therefore urged to provide mechanistic insights or additional
corroborative evidence to substantiate this key conclusion and enhance the overall
persuasiveness of the study.
Response: Thank you for this important comment. We agree that fully establishing
the causal relationship between TEVs and environmental adaptation would require
extensive functional validation experiments, which are beyond the scope of the
current study. In this work, we have focused on robust population genomic analyses to
identify putative adaptive TEVs and explore their potential roles in local adaptation
and responses to future climate change.
To provide additional mechanistic insights, we further analyzed the genomic context
of environment-associated variants to develop a preliminary regulatory framework
linking TEVs with potential modulation of gene expression. Using the PlantCARE
database, we predicted cis-regulatory elements, including promoter motifs and
transcription factor binding sites (TFBS). This framework suggests that TEV
insertions or linked variants near adaptive genes may alter local transcription factor
binding landscapes, thereby influencing gene expression responsiveness under
environmental stress. For example, we identified a long TE insertion upstream of
TLP3 that overlaps a predicted transcription factor binding site, as well as a SNP
upstream of ICE1 located within a putative regulatory motif. These findings suggest
that environment-associated variants could potentially modulate regulatory networks
(see revised Results and Supplementary Fig. S9). Our findings provide a valuable set
of testable hypotheses and candidate loci for future functional studies.
We have also toned down the wording in the manuscript to emphasize that our
findings provide evidence supporting a potential role of TEVs in local adaptation,
rather than definitive proof. While experimental validation is required to fully confirm
causality, the combined genomic and regulatory analyses presented here offer a
valuable resource and a set of candidate loci for future functional studies.
Supplementary Figure 9. b, Candidate adaptive TEV potentially affecting predicted
transcription factor binding site in the putative regulatory region of TLP3. The dashed
arrow represents the assumed regulation. The predicted transcription factor binding
site is depicted as red triangle. c, Candidate adaptive variants located within predicted
transcription factor binding site in the putative regulatory region of ICE1.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2: The authors have adequately addressed my concerns. I still have some quibbles about some of the wording, but I suspect that is due to differences between fields. My feeling is that authors, well, really, all of us, can forget that models are just models and linkage is just linkage. That being said, I congratulate the authors on what was almost certainly a difficult and complex task. One final caveat is the title: Transposable Element Jumping Facilitates Climate Change Adaptation in Wild Grapes. After all that back and forth, why make an unproven claim in the title? I would adjust the title to reflect the actual conclusions. Also, "jumping" is too informal, and really, the paper did not show that transposition caused anything. They showed that TE insertion variants are linked to loci that are associated with climate variability. I know, not as flashy, but best to stick to what we know.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Thank you for the authors’ thoughtful response. However, these replies still do not fully address my concerns. I remain skeptical regarding certain aspects of the data and the overall presentation of the article. Thus, additional work and further explanations are still required.
1. The authors explained that the environmental variables were sourced from WorldClim, with a resolution of 2.5 arcmin (approximately 5 km), and many samples share identical environmental data. I still have three key questions regarding this approach: First, are genotypic differences within a population also reflective of the population’s environmental adaptability? If so, can the impact of completely consistent environmental data on the analysis be effectively controlled? Second, according to the data provided by the authors, some samples exhibit elevation differences of up to 200 m or more (e.g., ZY407 – ZY416), which can induce notable microclimatic variations. Genotypic differences within the population are likely adaptive responses to these microclimatic differences. However, the use of identical environmental data for such samples in this study may introduce biases that affect the reliability of the analysis results. Finally, the authors stated that the data were downloaded from WorldClim, but it is critical to verify whether these data are representative of the specific year(s) when the samples were collected. Additionally, the WorldClim data used (covering 1970–2000) are over two decades old, and significant changes in current environmental conditions will inevitably compromise the accuracy of the analysis. For these reasons, I still maintain that environmental adaptability parameters inherent to the plants themselves should be adopted and incorporated into the analysis.
2. In this study, the authors identified candidate genes corresponding to bio3, 4, 10, 15, and 18. As noted, V. amurensis is considered as one of the most cold-tolerant grape species; however, this study lacks dedicated analysis of its cold resistance mechanisms—a trait that constitutes a key adaptive feature of V. amurensis and thus warrants inclusion in the research framework. Additionally, while the authors reported a large set of candidate genes, the absence of further analysis hinders the elucidation of how these genes collectively contribute to environmental adaptability. Further investigations are therefore required to validate and quantify the specific roles of these candidate genes in mediating the adaptive traits of V. amurensis. Moreover, although several genes associated with cold and drought tolerance were selected for detailed analysis, the study failed to clarify the specific impacts of transposon insertions on the structure or function of these genes. Without such mechanistic insights, the link between these genes and the adaptive phenotypes of V. amurensis remains insufficiently substantiated.
3. The title and research objective of this study focus on "Transposable Element Jumping Facilitates Climate Change Adaptation in Wild Grapes." However, it is clear that the authors have not provided sufficient evidence to support this core claim. The authors only demonstrated that TEVs are closely associated with several resistance-related genes. This association, however, does not directly confirm a causal link between TEVs and environmental adaptability. If the authors wish to argue that TEVs are key drivers of environmental adaptation, they must provide additional evidence to show that the overall pattern of TEV insertions enhances the adaptability of plants to their respective growing environments. Alternatively, if the authors propose that specific genes play a major role in TEV-mediated adaptation, they need to clarify how TEV insertions alter the expression of these target genes, and elucidate the mechanism by which such expression changes enable adaptation to different environmental conditions. Ultimately, the authors should provide a concise model to illustrate how TEV insertions influence environmental adaptability. This step is not only necessary to strengthen the study’s conclusions but also the core of this article.
4. The title of this article is "Transposable Element Jumping Facilitates Climate Change Adaptation in Wild Grapes"; however, the study primarily focuses on analyzing the environmental adaptation mechanisms of V. amurensis. Since this proposed mechanism has not been validated or extended to other wild grape species, the title’s broad claim regarding "wild grapes" is somewhat overgeneralized and thus inappropriate. To address this discrepancy, the authors should either conduct comparable analyses on additional wild grape taxa to verify the universality of the mechanism, or revise the title to more accurately reflect the study’s focal species and avoid overextrapolation.

Response to Review Comments
Part I: Summary of responses to the major questions:
We sincerely appreciate the careful evaluation by the editor and the three reviewers.
Before presenting a detailed point-by-point response in Part II, we first address four
major issues collectively:
First, revision of the manuscript title based on the combined feedback from all
three reviewers: In response to the reviewers’ collective concerns regarding
overstatement, we revised the title to: “Transposable Elements Contribute to Climate
Change Adaptation in the Wild Amur Grape (Vitis amurensis)”.
Second, comprehensive language editing to improve clarity and readability: We
have carefully revised the manuscript according to reviewer’s suggestions and we have
further reviewed and refined the entire manuscript to improve consistency, clarity, and
grammatical accuracy.
Third, clarification of the appropriateness of the environmental data: We clarified
that the population-level GEA framework used in this study targets broad-scale and
long-term environmental gradients among populations. The suitability of data from
WorldClim for this purpose, particularly for long-lived perennial species, was justified
with reference to its widespread use in population genomic studies.
Fourth, expansion of functional interpretation and clarification of study scope: We
performed a GO enrichment analysis of 823 candidate genes, revealing significant
enrichments in cold- and drought-response pathways. We also expanded the discussion
of cold resistance mechanisms by integrating literature-supported evidence and
considering the potential impact of TEVs. We clarified that experimental validation
remains beyond the scope of this study.
In conclusion, we have provided detailed explanations in response to the reviewers'
comments. All updates in the manuscript are highlighted with tracked changes.
Additionally, we have revised the manuscript and supplemental tables.
